item.title: Carolina Panthers 2026 fan mailbag: Eagles woes, Panthers offensive gameplay, Bryce Young extension, and more!
item.description: Answering all your questions in this week’s fan mailbag!
item.content:encoded:
Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We’re right back into Panthers football with a very winnable matchup on Sunday, albeit due to many injuries in Philadelphia. But the game keeps rolling and the cards keep getting dealt, all we can do is enjoy the fun of the regular season. Let’s dive into your questions!

JoshuaTreeTD: Do you think Dave and Brad will continue to switch up the offensive play style to attack any given opponents weakness from week to week? It felt like the Lions were not expecting such heavy RPO plays and it caught them fully off guard and Bryce executed it almost perfectly. What would you predict the play style will be to attack Philly?

The Panthers have definitely been adaptive on offense. I think the formula of mixing in some deep shots with their usual run approach will continue, but I definitely see them running a lot of RPO this week against a pretty good Eagles front seven. This offense has been aggressive as far as trying to score points, so I do think I agree that they’ll have a unique game plan for each team they face. And that seemed to be the vision when they brought in Dave Canales.

schrodingersblackcat: Will Bryce be the one to finally break our black jersey curse?

I didn’t feel great about this game, but then Jalen Hurts was ruled out with a blood clot. Which, by the way, from one fan base to another, I hope he recovers in short order and has no complications. These types of things make you realize there’s more to life than the next week of football, and I hope Hurts gets all the treatment he needs and doesn’t have any negative impact on his life as a person.

That said, this is definitely a game where the Panthers should have every chance to win it, in convincing fashion. And knowing their recent history as a franchise, they might drop the ball and lose this game. Cause Panthers fans can never have nice things.

Aleins4u: If you had a offensive oriented head coach, would you rather:

  1. Have a good, but not great DC, who frequently gets HC interviews but never gets the job
  2. A series of great DCs, but each only lasts 2 years before getting poached for a HC job

And same question, except a defensive oriented head coach and OCs.

The core of the question is, would you rather a good quality, consistent approach on the side of the ball the HC has less knowledge about, or a constantly but shifting great approach that might require different player types.

I’m all for having coordinators on both sides of the ball that are so good that they move on to higher positions. I think you have to maximize every coach you have, because they can be poached at any moment. I would rather have coordinators that prove themselves worthy of going off to make more money and take on more responsibility, because the best franchises in the NFL tend to expect this and try to give development reps to the guys they have in the trenches behind them. I’d much rather have a coordinator that helps this team win a Super Bowl than someone who isn’t excellent enough to get them there, but still sticks around because other teams don’t feel he can take them to the next level. The name of the game is winning in this league, win the championship and figure out the repercussions after the fact.

Mozzie11: The NFC South has been the worst division for years with winners having losing records at times. This year the NFC East is throwing their hat the ring for worst. Panthers and Eagles is just part of the epic battle. Which division ‘wins’ the title this year?

I do think the NFC South will continue its recent history of getting the least deserving team a playoff berth. The Panthers have been very good, but they are still up and down. The Falcons are on an upward trajectory. The Saints are 2-3 unexpected wins away from joining them at the top of the division. The NFC East is certainly in the same playing field, but I think one of those teams will jump far ahead of the rest. Which team that is at this juncture, I don’t know.

@WTMealey: Are we eyeballing the entire NFC playoff picture now or just the South?

Like is it silly to be glad the Rams lost last night? BTW do we have rivalry with them now?

But really are we rooting for AFC teams to beat top 10 NFC teams to help our likelihood of having 2 home playoff games or ….? Is it too soon?

I think bolshy in the comments answered this better than I could: “I wouldn’t eyeball anything but Philly right now”. This Panthers team is showing a great deal if promise, but I’d be more concerned with the games they win than other contenders losing. They may change that mindset in the coming weeks, but I’m not ready to do that right now. I’ve been hurt too many times.

Brazilian Panther: Pick one between the OG movie Carrie from 76, the remake with Chloe Grace Moretz from 2013 or Mike Flanagan’s 2026 mini series on Prime Video Brian. I just watched the series this past weekend and I really liked what they came up with. Cheers

To be fully transparent, I haven’t watched even a little of the new mini-series. So I can’t make a ruling on that, but I’ve heard nothing but good things about it. Sound off down below in the comments if you have, and what your thoughts on it. I’m very much a fan of the original, but I liked both of the first two iterations.

casualpanthersfan: The panthers are currently averaging 30.3 point per game. Would you take the over or under on the panthers point total this week?

I will always preface these questions with the same statement; I do not bet real money on the Panthers because they always do the opposite of what I think. And if I think they’ll do the opposite of what the regular media thinks they’ll do, I also lose most of the time. Don’t bet on the Panthers, your mental health will thank you.

But gun to my head, this is still a strong Eagles defense. I think it will be an ugly low scoring game.

Bruce Guild: Brian, we’re giving up 5.4 yards a carry so far, but Philly just lost Lane Johnson to retirement, traded Jurgens, has Dickerson on IR, and ran for only 22 yards in London without Saquon. Is this the week Evero’s front finally gets right against the run, or does our run D get exposed anyway? And with both starting corners on IR, do they load the box, make Hurts beat them throwing, and trust Will Lee and Evans one-on-one?

This week will be interesting, and thank you for the Grok question. Jalen Hurts suddenly being out changes the whole dynamic of this game, and I’m not sure if Saquon Barkley or Devonta Smith ends up playing given this development. They are both banged up and the Eagles might elect to just rest them both because of the dire situation. But if the Eagles do come out aggressive, I expect Ejiro Evero to be very aggressive blitzing like he has been this season. And if Saquon plays I expect the focus will be to contain him, just like the focus against the Lions and Gibbs.

Bull123: Injuries…who plays on OL?…Coker?…Phillips? Are we stuck with Evans?

Seems like Taylor Moton could be back, but I think the coaching staff plays it safe with him after his health issues. Monroe Freeling is still dealing with his knee issue in week 4, and while he got a limited practice on Thursday I don’t know where he’s at. So we might be seeing Stone Forsythe starting just to not rush anyone back. I expect the guard situation on the OL to remain the same. Jalen Coker is all go for Sunday. We’ll have to wait on Jaelan Phillips but he’s logged two limited practices this week. I assume you’re referring to Akayleb Evans with the last part, and I don’t expect his role to change too much. The Panthers seem to be wading out this period of having their top 2 CBs hurt until mid season.

LouWillVille: Once Moton and Freeling are both cleared to play do you think Freeling becomes the swing tackle or is there a chance he takes over at LT for Walker?

Also, with Cam Jackson out for the year would you expect a trade for some IDL depth? Obviously, we’re getting Wharton back, but he has been injury prone and even with him the depth is thin.

I do think once Taylor Moton is full go, they keep Monroe Freeling on the bench for a bit. That was always the plan if he didn’t win the LT job from Rasheed Walker, and he basically spent the entire preseason/training camp period taking reps at right tackle, transitioning back to playing left tackle after all of that time isn’t going to happen overnight.

As far as the DL goes, they could maybe make a trade for a relatively low cost interior guy who is more run stuffing focused, but I don’t expect them to do anything crazy. They very well might just roll with Turk Wharton, Aaron Hall, and Bobby Brown Jr to compliment Derrick Brown. And that combination might be just fine.

Irishboy: Brian, as we are coming off the bye week, I know Bryce did a lot of travelling/TV work during the week off. Could any of this, including the MVP chants have any impact into how prepared and how he plays for Sunday? Myself, I am hoping not, but this is a lot of positive noise that he hasn’t received since coming into the league.

I’m not worried at all about Bryce Young taking some media time during the bye week. The team still had their own practice and workout time, the bye week is all about just taking some time off to recover and reload. Bryce has never struck me as the type to come in mentally unprepared for a game. I’m glad he’s getting some flowers rather than being labeled a tremendous bust. This stuff might actually help him continue to be confident in his game now that outside sources are recognizing how excellent he has been in 4 games this year.

Highmiles: Late question, since Bryce has become a key element of our offense, how will he hold up physically? I worried he would be injured When he started his NFL career, but he has done well staying on the field. Now that he is showing out as our QB he will probably be a more frequent target of the defenses. Is he going to be able to handle it physically?

Aside from relatively routine minor injuries, Bryce Young has survived quite a few beatings in his career so far. I am not concerned at all with the ankle injuries that have kept him out for a game or so during his time as an NFL starter. He’s proven he’s tough and he’s generally pretty smart about avoiding non-essential contact. I am not concerned at all.

RealityDan: Simple question, no worries if it’s too late to answer, but if BY ends the season for the most part sustaining what he’s already done through the rest of the season, what kind of extension numbers are we looking at? I know 55m per year has been thrown around a lot, but my thoughts are that Baker just got that. If we’re talking of doing this in the offseason, this assumes that other QBs like Stroud, Murray if he plays well, etc. are also getting contracts inked, could we be talking 60-plus per year for BY? And for how many years and how much guaranteed?

If Bryce continues to lead the league in most passing categories, he’s getting $60+ mil per year and there’s really nothing to talk about. Probably at least 5 years just because that’s how new QB contracts are often structured in a situation like this. The average amount per year doesn’t really matter as much as how they structure it from a guaranteed money/signing bonus/dead money standpoint. If they extend him and he continues to play well, those numbers all go out the window with restructures and a potential extension two to three years into that next deal. If he’s playing at this level throughout that time, the numbers won’t matter a whole lot aside from how long the Panthers take to give him the next bite of the apple.

That’s all for this week, Panthers fans. Join us next week for another edition of the fan mailbag. KEEP POUNDING!

item.title: What to know about Falcons – Bears in Week 6
item.description: The Falcons face another banged-up team, this one a Chicago squad looking to bounce back after an ugly loss of their own.
item.content:encoded:
The Falcons just a heartbreaker in overtime to the Ravens. The Bears got absolutely drubbed by a divisional rival. Both of these teams are looking for a win, but naturally, only one can get it. Will it be the Falcons?

That’s a question with a lot of moving parts. If the Bears don’t start Caleb Williams, my instinct is that yes, a Chicago team with a backup quarterback and no Kyle Monangai is quite gettable for Atlanta. If Williams is back in action and Monangai is too, this offense is incredibly formidable, and that looks to be the way things are trending for the Bears. That makes the task much harder, even if the shaky Bears defense also provides real opportunities.

How will this one go? That remains to be seen, but here’s what you need to know for Week 6.

Team rankings

The Bears are one of those teams that look extremely impressive on paper and are very talented, but have more weaknesses than these surface level metrics might indicate. The passing attack is lesser without Caleb Williams, the rushing attack is incredible but may be missing sledgehammer back Kyle Monangai this week. The defense, meanwhile, has struggled against good offenses and been lights out against bad ones, and is also dealing with injuries. The have one of the brightest offensive minds in football and a very good team top to bottom when they’re fully healthy, but they are not fully healthy.

Atlanta’s been up-and-down but is settling into roughly the shape I think we’ll see this season, which is a very good offense with an effective defense that isn’t quite good enough to stop elite passing games or rushing attacks. The injuries in the secondary and attrition up front have combined to make the sledding tougher and they’re not forcing enough turnovers, but overall this looks like a team that should be comfortably league average or better across these high level categories. They just need to settle into a consistent level of play.

How the Bears have changed in 2026

They returned a ton of talent from last year, and notably traded Gervon Dexter to the Falcons and re-united him with ex-Bears assistant general manager Ian Cunningham, who is now running the show in Atlanta. They sought to bolster the defense in particular with signings like safety Coby Bryant, defensive tackles Kentavius Street and Neville Gallimore, and linebacker Devin Bush. Their draft brought in promising safety Dillon Thieneman, center Logan Jones, and some interesting depth.

Overall, though, this was not a transformative offseason and was not intended to be, as the Bears built a solid foundation of talent and were betting on good coaching and some truly outstanding potential on offense to push them over the top this year.

What to know for Week 6

The Bears are an incredibly dangerous offense paired with a defense that is worse than its underlying metrics suggest. That offers up a recipe for a real shootout in Atlanta.

It’s tough to get a read on the actual abilities of this Bears team, but the offense was at full strength in Week 1 in favorable conditions and boatraced the Panthers, putting up 552 yards en route to a 59-37 win. The following week, they played the Vikings in the rain and Brian Flores befuddled Chicago, which lost 9-3 and lost Williams for multiple weeks. It’s been difficult to get a true sense of the offense from there because they’ve had Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent under center and have had running back injuries, as well, but Ben Johnson did dismantle the Eagles 27-7 in Week 3 with Keenum.

With Williams set to return, a world of possibilities opens up for Chicago again. He’s simply one of the most gifted quarterbacks in league, and if the results can be a bit inconsistent, Williams’ ability to make nearly any throw while backpedaling away from pressure, scrambling, or otherwise just being wildly off-balance makes defending him extraordinarily difficult. The fact that the Falcons have not yet faced him adds a little difficulty to the mix, as does the fact that he can be a lethal scrambler.

Williams has plenty of weapons to throw to. While they take turns popping off, Luther Burden, Rome Odunze, and Kalif Raymond offer plenty of speed and big play potential; tight ends Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet are both capable pass catchers as well. Ben Johnson is a mad scientist who marries that varied passing attack to a very strong ground game featuring D’Andre Swift—who is banged up—and bowling ball with legs Kyle Monangai, who seems likely to miss this game. Teams that can’t account for all these threats tend to have a tough time, and the Falcons are a bit banged up in the secondary.

Pressure is the best way to solve this. This is not a Tyler Huntley game, where the Falcons leaned heavily on the blitz and paid for it against the Ravens backup, who has the third-best completion percentage when pressured in the NFL this year. Williams is 22nd in the NFL in completion percentage under pressure, plummeting 30 percentage points when the rush is getting to him, though he remains a threat to break a long run. Williams does not take many sacks, but you’ll live with that if you can force him into bad throws. If that puts extra pressure on a ground game that’s much less effective with a banged-up Swift and without Monangai, so much the better.

The Falcons defense will have its work cut out for it regardless, but what about the Falcons offense? That’s a little more straightforward, despite Chicago being statistically top ten thus far through five weeks.

What do I mean by that? Chicago has faced two capable offenses thus far and allowed over 30 points to both; the Panthers scored 37 in a shootout and the Packers easily set a new season high with 31 points last week. They held the Jets, Vikings, and Eagles in check, but all three of those teams are struggling with personnel troubles and dysfunction, so that’s not an achievement that deserves sustained applause.

The splits here are also reflected in passing yardage, where Bryce Young and Jordan Love picked them apart for over 300 yards apiece, while Geno Smith, Carson Wentz, and Jalen Hurts in whatever nightmare box the Eagles are putting in all scuffled. The Bears have a run defense that looks better in raw yardage than in DVOA, and they have yet to face a back as good as Bijan Robinson (and arguably not even as good as Brian Robinson Jr., for that matter). They can rush the passer well and have a knack for authoring big plays, but they also lost leading sack artists Montez Sweat and Dayo Odeyingbo for this week alongside linebacker TJ Edwards, leaving them thinner and less capable up front.

As long as Michael Penix Jr. is good to go, this offense is more than capable of attacking this Chicago defense deep and with a diet of the Robinsons, which is likely to bear real fruit. The bigger question is whether this Falcons defense can bottle up a very capable, creative Bears offense and, failing that, whether the offense can keep up with what the Bears are capable of doing. I would be very surprised if this doesn’t turn into a shootout, unless Williams or Penix suffers an unexpected setback and don’t play Sunday.

The Falcons badly need to get back on track after that sour Sunday night and have a real chance to do so against yet another depleted team. If they can’t get the job done against a much less effective defense and a team that might be working without one of its top backs and with a limited or absent version of their star young quarterback, it’s going to be time to worry.

item.title: It might not be possible for Bills to “win” against Raiders
item.description: I mean, of course they can win and there’s no reason to think they can’t, but…
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills will be in Las Vegas this weekend to take on the Raiders and they may quite possibly be facing a “no-won” situation. Now, I know what you’re thinking. What the heck, Skare? The Bills are favored by 4.5 – 5.5 points against the Raiders and that says volumes, especially when the opponent literally resides in the home of “the books” that set those odds.

OK. Fine. You got me. I’m not talking about the scoreboard, where I agree with the oddsmakers. Buffalo can definitely win the actual game. But we’re fans. There’s more to it than that and I don’t like this week because I don’t see an easy path for us to win…

The Narrative

It’s never too early to start thinking about the division and that’s currently a two-team race in the AFC East. While Buffalo currently leads the way, the New England Patriots are nipping at the Bills’ heels with a head-to-head win already. As of right now, we can’t let them pull even.

Yes, Buffalo controls their own destiny. Just keep winning and all is well in the standings but for now, we can’t escape the narratives. The Patriots made it to a Super Bowl before Josh Allen, a fact I detest. That’s led to all sorts of chatter, including opposing fans besmirching Allen and company who have been consistently excellent for what has now become ages.

That’s a huge part of the game for fans and I have a lot more fun when we’re more firmly on top. Against the Raiders, it’s going to take a lot to avoid that annoying chatter from increasing.

I sat around last Sunday hoping the 3 – 1 team from Las Vegas would put the 2 – 2 Patriots below .500, and I’m thinking Rumblers readers were too. Not only didn’t that happen, but the Raiders were flat out embarrassed by New England. Drake Maye threw for 374 with a near perfect passer rating and four touchdowns to zero interceptions.

Not only are the Raiders a common opponent between us and the Pats, but it’s happening in back to back weeks and it’s a comparison league. If we don’t beat the **** out of the Raiders, it’s only going to fuel the irritating chatter.

The Raiders allowed scores on seven out of ten drives. All but one of those drives was a touchdown. Their secondary allowed Maye 11 yards per passing attempt. Look at this passing chart!

It only gets more grim when you factor in the other side of the ball. It wasn’t like it was a shootout. The final score was 45 – 17 and one of the Raiders’ touchdowns was definitively garbage time.

So yes, the Bills are a game ahead, but to keep the chatter at bay they’re going to need to win convincingly. The Bills should be expected to win, but the Raiders are still a 3 – 2 team. Yes the wins come against teams that are a combined 1 – 14 (Dolphins, Chargers, and Saints). But they’re still wins. The Raiders also fought Kansas City to the end, losing by just a field goal.

For now, we may have to resign ourselves to a little more irritating chirping.

item.title: Giants’ DC Dennard Wilson: ‘We like playing with a chip on our shoulder’
item.description: NY Giants defensive coordinator on the Giants’ aggressive defense
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants are 3-1-1 and in the driver’s seat of the NFC East. They might not have won in Week 5, but they also didn’t lose and still managed to expand their lead in the division by half a game. While the story of Week 1 as the Giants’ suffocating offense, the story of the last three games has been the defense.

The Giants have been led by defense over the last 7 quarters, with Dennard Wilson switching to an aggressive blitzing front. The Giants now lead the NFL in Cover-0 (pure man coverage across the board) and are second in the NFL in in blitz rate over the last two weeks.

Their defense has been impressive and it’s been leading to wins — the Giants haven’t lost since starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the season.

Yet for the third game in a row, the NFC East leading Giants are underdogs against a cellar-dweller. And much of the national media is once again is picking the Giants’ opponents over the division leader.

“Everybody counts us out,” defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said Thursday. “We like playing with a chip on our shoulder. That’s what it is.”

On the Giants’ blitzing attack

The Giants made a significant adjustment in the second quarter against the Arizona Cardinals and it was a minor revolution for the defense. The Giants had spent the first 13 quarters of the season relying on their athletic edge defenders to win on their own, and not blitzing often. After the Cardinals carved them up in the first quarter of Week 3, the Giants started sending pressure and it changed their entire defense.

“It’s been effective,” Wilson said. “I mean, we’ve been able to hit the quarterback. We’ve been able to disguise. They don’t know where it’s coming from. And the biggest thing when you pressure, the DB’s are covering well so you have more confidence in calling it. They’ve been doing a good job on the back end, communicating, playing man-to-man, playing fire zone coverage. So, it’s been good for us. It’s been effective and we’ve been getting the quarterback off the spot and forcing them to bad decisions.”

It’s almost a surprise that the Giants waited as long as they did to unleash their blitz package. Perhaps the weather slowed them down against the Tennessee Titans, but Wilson certainly seems happy to be blitzing now.

“I like everybody blitzing,” Wilson said. “On our defense, everybody’s a blitzer. Dru is a dynamic player. Dru, let’s talk a little bit about [CB] Dru (Phillips) and his growth. Dru has been playing some really good, high-level football the last three or four weeks in coverage, blitzing, playing the run. He’s ahead of things. I love where he’s at, but he is an asset. He is an explosive, he’s another violent player that’s not afraid of contact. And when we get the opportunity to send him or any other player that we have, we work on it, we rep it, and they go full speed and you don’t know where it’s going to come from.”

“One thing I like about this group, they love going forward,” he added. “They love attacking. So, they all are attack players. So, in our scheme, we have the ability to run blitzes from everywhere and anybody can come from different looks. And that’s the enjoyment of being in this system, running this system, and also the players fitting within the system. So, they can come from anywhere.”

In particular, the Giants’ blitzes have unleashed rookie linebacker Arvell Reese, who has quickly become one of the most dynamic defenders in the NFL. For his part, Wilson relishes the opportunities to get Reese going forward and matched up on smaller blockers.

“If you can get Arvell on a running back, it’s a good matchup for us any day of the week,” Wilson said. “He is a violent scud missile. When he goes forward, I say he’s like a bull, he’s sees red and it’s good for us. If we can dictate and get a running back and get him on a one-on-one, more times than not he’s going to win. And if the first time that he goes, he’s going to make you feel him. And if he can make you feel him and then he’s already elusive and a hell of an athlete, so now they can set him up with moves and things like that. So, it’s always fun to turn on the film and see Arvell when he makes contact with people because it doesn’t look good.”

On the defense against the Washington Commanders

The Giants were generally very good against the Washington Commanders, but they had a couple lapses. In particular were the two long scrambles by QB Jayden Daniels. Wilson said Thursday that neither play should have happened.

“Well, first and foremost, both of them (QB Jayden Daniels’ runs) should never have happened,” Wilson said. “We had a five-man front with a game, and we didn’t execute the game. And when we didn’t execute the game, we didn’t have a guy wrap. And if the guy wrapped, he would have been right in his face. And then on the second one, it’s about balancing the rush. You can’t have two interior tackles outside of the hash. And we didn’t get vertical penetration, and he got out. Both situations, the one on the first touchdown, it was a second and six, right? And we always talk about you can spy, and we had a spy in the game but on second down, are you spying when you’re really trying to go pressure them there? But for us, in the run game and with the quarterback scrambling, it’s about our execution. It’s about everybody doing their job when their number’s called. The first run that popped should have never popped either. They had we call a plunge play with the tight end going back, and we had three guys behind the ball. When that happens and they flash back, the three guys got to work in unison to rock back, and we didn’t. And that starts from communication. That starts from eye discipline. That’s being ahead of the play, but we’ll get that fixed. And for the most part, we’ve been pretty good at it but we can’t have those lapses. And we’ve been communicating with the players a lot about this. It’s like if you just do your job and don’t worry about anything else and you take care of your responsibility, we play really good defense. When one guy gets out of whack, this or that, things happen. Also on those plays, we got to get them down in the secondary. And ultimately if things pop, we got to get them down in the secondary. But we worked diligently this week just making sure our communication is loud, it’s obnoxious, it’s annoying, and making sure that we surround the ball this week going into this game.”

Daniels’ two touchdowns were mistakes by the Giants, and the offense would have done more than enough (eventually) to win if the defense had shut Daniels down. But for the third game in a row, the defense ultimately made the play to win (or at least not-lose) the game. In this case, Wilson credited Kayvon Thibodeaux and Darius Alexander for heads-up plays to slow the Commanders down and burn the closing seconds of overtime.

“Well, I think it all goes back to the whole unit with the situational awareness,” Wilson said. “Harbs (John Harbaugh) does a great job, and we’ve been in that situation before in practice, that we’ve practiced that and how to handle it. But let’s go back to that play, I mean, without Thibs (edge defender Kayvon Thibodeaux) making that play and forcing the quarterback to go down when he added to him, that play wouldn’t have happened. So, it’s just kudos to all of them. (DL) Darius (Alexander) was very good on that play too, trying to hold things up. So, it was a lot of situational awareness there and obviously, I wish we got it done before that instead of having a tie. But the guys, they bowed up in that fourth quarter. They didn’t waver. They attacked the moment from everybody on defense. And I just love their tenacity and the way they know how to finish.

“The key for us is just to execute,” he added, “to communicate, get the call, get aligned, beat them into a stance, and then line up and play our style of football.”

item.title: Bengals Film Room: Joe Burrow has season-best performance vs. Miami Dolphins
item.description: Efficiency and balance are keys for Burrow and the Bengals offense going forward.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time this season, we saw peak Joe Burrow as he led the Cincinnati Bengals to a 31-24 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 5.

The passing numbers a week prior against Jacksonville showed 428 yards passing with 1 passing touchdown and 2 interceptions. While he played pretty well overall, the turnovers played a big part in the Bengals coming up short against the Jaguars.

This week against Miami, Burrow threw for just 190 yards on the day. To me, it was a better performance than the week before. Mainly, the reason for that is that he didn’t have a single turnover. When the Bengals can win the turnover battle, they are going to win a lot of games. They were also able to have more balance with the running game this week, getting 117 rushing yards on Sunday.

Burrow finished the game against Miami completing 23/32 passes on the day for a 71.9% completion rate. He also was able to throw for 4 touchdown passes, with three of those coming in the first half. He threw those three touchdowns to Mike Gesicki, Samaje Perine, and Tanner Hudson. All three of those scores came inside the red zone.

Finding ways to finish with touchdowns instead of field goals in the red zone is going to continue being a critical component of how successful this team is on a weekly basis.

Burrow was able to spread the wealth on Miami, with nine different players catching a pass this week. While that is always beneficial, it is still nice to have Ja’Marr Chase back on the field. Chase missed a good chunk of the previous game with a concussion, but was able to get cleared and showed no signs of that slowing him down against the Dolphins. Burrow did a masterful job maneuvering in the pocket for his final touchdown pass. This time finding Ja’Marr Chase for a 45-yard touchdown score. Chase was able to pin the ball up by his shoulder with one hand.

The Burrow to Chase connection is alive and well, and they will need it to be on point after the bye week. The Bengals will travel to division leading Baltimore on October 25th. An efficient Joe Burrow could help the Bengals secure a huge divisional road win that day.

The rebuilding Titans are in full-blown evaluation mode. Continuing to evaluate the young talents on this roster has become the most important must-achieve in yet another wasted campaign. We’ve identified three young Titans who are most worth analyzing versus the Colts in Week 6.

QB Cam Ward

Titans QB Cam Ward was a mixed bag versus the Houston Texans. Ward also made a few off-script plays, but was occasionally indecisive while bailing clean pockets. WR Carnell Tate

Rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate failed to build on his breakout performance. After registering nine receptions on 12 targets for 145 yards versus the Baltimore Ravens in Week 4, he had just one catch for six yards against the Texans. It’s criminal that Tate only had five targets, but Texans CB Derek Stingley Jr. did a great job eliminating him. The Titans need to pepper their fourth overall pick with targets in this Colts game.

LB Anthony Hill Jr.

Rookie linebacker Anthony Hill Jr. has arguably written the most positive story of this miserable 2026 Titans season. The former Texas Longhorns standout has posted a team-high 47 tackles. In fact, Hill ranks sixth in the entire NFL in tackles. He’s displaying a sideline-to-sideline skill set and is currently thriving in Robert Saleh’s defense. item.title: Dolphins news: Should Miami stay away from Jeremiah Smith in the 2027 NFL Draft?
item.description: A collection of Miami Dolphins news from around the web, including maybe not selecting Jeremiah Smith in the 2027 NFL Draft.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins have started the 2026 NFL season with five straight losses and look like a team in contention for the first-overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. The Dolphins are in the early stages of a complete franchise rebuild and, while the win column still shows a zero, there have been signs of growth for an incredibly young, inexperienced team.

There is hope for the Dolphins’ future, but they will likely continue to struggle in the near term as they return from their bye next week. With that first pick on the table, Dolphins fans have already started looking toward the Draft and the prospects that could land on Miami’s board. One name has leapt to the top of the wish list: Ohio State wide receiver Jaremiah Smith. The dynamic pass catcher could prove to be a key offensive weapon in the NFL, and he might become just the fourth wide receiver to be taken first overall in the draft.

But Miami Dolphins on SI writer Alain Poupart thinks the Dolphins may want to hit the brakes on the idea of selecting Smith:

The previous 10 [Super Bowl] winners — Kansas City three times, Philadelphia and New England twice, Tampa Bay, the L.A. Rams and most recently Seattle — featured in their starting lineup a total of 13 players who entered the NFL as a top 5 pick.

Only one of them was a wide receiver. And that wide receiver, Sammy Watkins of the Kansas City Chiefs in 2019, wasn’t drafted by that team, but rather by the Buffalo Bills five years earlier.

Poupart goes on to look at other star receivers, including Hall of Famer Calvin Johnson and Miami’s former duo of Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle, and the lack of playoff success that came with them. Smith might be an exceptional talent in the NFL, but should Miami address a different position rather than betting on a wide receiver to spark the rebuild in 2027?

The New York Jets’ biggest rival in the AFC East is the New England Patriots. The Patriots probably don’t feel the same way, which only makes this game more intense from a Gang Green perspective.

New England has been giving the Jets the business for a long time.

If you combine those previous pair of Smith performances, he has thrown for 689 passing yards, has a two-to-one touchdown-to-interception ratio, and has averaged a 72.8% completion percentage.

item.title: #PostPulpit mailbag: How can Drake Maye attack the Jets?
item.description: The latest edition of our Patriots mailbag answers questions about the Jets matchup, running game, and more.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots are looking to keep their winning streak alive as they welcome the New York Jets to Gillette Stadium.

So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag.

How would you attack the Jets defense? – Maye The Force Be With You

What’s different about the Jets this year that would help them avoid another drubbing like they got at the end of last year? – paulnewman

As he did with his defenses in Detroit, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn wants his defense to play man coverage and blitz. Through the season, New York ranks second in blitz rate and 10th in man coverage rate.

However, that approach could be costly against Drake Maye, who has excelled against the blitz and can exploit man coverage by pushing the ball downfield or making plays with his legs. If the Jets lean heavily on single-high coverages, expect Maye to take his shots, as he did last week.

The most notable change for the Jets this season has been Glenn’s increased versatility on defense. New York is leaning more heavily into split-safety coverages, including a significant increase in Cover 6, and could feature those looks Sunday to limit Maye’s deep-ball opportunities.

While there isn’t much to fear from the Jets’ offense from this perspective with Christian Gonzalez available to limit Garrett Wilson, New York has also overhauled its defensive personnel this offseason, potentially setting the stage for a low-scoring divisional battle. Rookie David Bailey has gotten off to a fast start on the edge, while veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick is still making plays in the backend.

With Henderson being out a few weeks, how do you see the offense compensating for that? More Stevens, Corey Kiner increased load, or perhaps getting our younger WR’s more involved by adding more 4-5 WR sets & spreading out opposing D’s? – KissBillsRings

With Henderson out for sometime, could we see Larison called up? – jpd985

We’ll see if Henderson misses time after somehow logging a pair of limited practices this week. If he’s out Sunday, Rhamondre Stevenson should be expected to carry the load, as he did in the regular-season opener when he played 60 snaps with Henderson sidelined.

Behind Stevenson, Larison would likely be elevated from the practice squad again, as he was in Week 1, with Kiner handling the change-of-pace carries. While the fumble is something a depth running back can’t afford, I thought Kiner actually ran well against the Raiders last week.

If Yahoo’s stats are right, the Pats are 11th in the league in rushing yards/game at 121.6, and 16th in the league in rushing yards/attempt at 4.1yd/att. So they’re persistent?

With Gilliam and Henderson laid up, and a Jets team begging for jumbo packages running down their throat to wear down their talented defensive line, what do the Pats have to do to improve rushing efficiency? – WannaBe Pats GM

More of what they’ve done the last two weeks. After a slow start on the ground this season, the Patriots have changed things up and become less predictable scheme wise. They’ve spiced up their go-to ground game with more motion and window dressing and have leaned into new schemes as well.

With much being written about how Maye couldn’t handle the 2 high safety looks from last year’s playoffs and the first few games of this season, what has changed? Did BUF and LV not play those looks or have worse personnel? Or are there signs that Maye is starting to handle that better? – Palm_Fronds_and_Shamrocks

Maye ranked near the top of the league in several metrics against Cover 2 last regular season. However, given his exceptional deep-ball efficiency, it was — and still is — viewed as one of the best strategies for limiting explosive plays.

The issues in the playoffs seemed to stem more from the quality of opposing defenses than from the schemes themselves. Maye hasn’t had many issues against those coverages in recent weeks, although it was puzzling to see Las Vegas opt for the opposite strategy and play single-high man coverage on more than 50% of its drop backs — a risky approach against a quarterback like Maye.

Were you excited to finally see the Patriots use Pop Douglas & Kyle Williams correctly against the Raiders leading to 3 TD’s and 156 Yards combined? – For Pats Sake

The usage didn’t really change for DeMario Douglas and Kyle Williams last week. Douglas scored two touchdowns against busted coverages and ran a pair of really strong routes.

Williams, meanwhile, finally got opportunities to make plays downfield against a Las Vegas defense that played single-high safety on more than 50% of its snaps. He capitalized.

Considering the injury bug that hit our team until now, who would be the 8 IR players you think should be brought back during the regular season? What about the extra two players, after we go into the playoffs? Would you wait with the last 2-3 spots closer to the playoffs to see if a certain position needs more help than others (say CB instead of WR)? – Maxxwell

This is something the Patriots will have to manage moving forward when it comes to their roster. They have already used two return designations on Marcus Bryant and Brenden Schooler, with A.J. Brown set to take the third.

Of the remaining players on injured reserve, Mack Hollins and Reggie Gilliam should be considered likely candidates for two more spots. From there, the Patriots can remain flexible with the final three regular-season return designations, plus two additional spots in the playoffs, as no other player on IR appears to be an immediate priority to return.

That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow@iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

item.title: Cowboys news: Mike Pettine should bring change to the defense
item.description: Here is today’s Dallas Cowboys news.
item.content:encoded:
The talk around the Dallas Cowboys after another disappointing start to the 2026 season remains rather pessimistic.

But just a few days ahead of their trip to Lambeau to take on the Green Bay Packers, most of the conversations are centered around the hiring of long-time defensive coach Mike Pettine. With a new veteran defensive coach on staff, there is some hope that the Cowboys defense can turn things around. They will get a good shot on Sunday night to prove themselves against a solid Green Bay offense coming off the best game of their season so far.

Christian Parker ‘likely’ to remain coaching on field, talks Mike Pettine hire – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com

After Jerry Jones said on 105.3 The Fan that Christian Parker would be moving to the booth, both Parker and Brian Schottenheimer denied that rumor. With Parker still likely to be on the sideline, the question now is, where will Mike Pettine be?

Earlier in the week, Cowboys owner/GM Jerry Jones said on 105.3 The Fan that defensive coordinator Christian Parker would be moving from the sidelines up to the coaches booth to call the defense.

As the week has gone on, it appears that may not be the case. Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said Wednesday “none of those decisions have been finalized,”  and Parker had a good chance to remain on the field. On Thursday, Parker reiterated that sentiment.

“Still working through some of that, but [I’ll] most likely going to be down [on the field] still.” Parker said on Thursday.

2 Cowboys Miss Thursday Practice, DeMarvion Overshown Progressing In New Injury Report – Josh Sanchez, SI.com

The Cowboys defense continues to be banged up, but it looks like they may get some reinforcements back in week six. After a nice showing in week five, Ameer Speed returns to the practice field in limited fashion, as well as Joey Porter Jr. While Cobie Durant is still not expected to return, the Cowboys secondary is inching towards full strength in the coming weeks.

On Thursday afternoon, the Cowboys returned to the practice field and dropped their latest injury report. On Wednesday, five players did not participate in practice, but on Thursday, that number was down to two.

The good news for Dallas is that starting linebacker DeMarvion Overshown is making progress and taking a step toward returning to the field, while veteran linebacker Von Miller also returned after a rest day and cornerback Ameer Speed was upgraded to limited.

With Malachi Lawrence expected to see an uptick in playing time, someone’s playing time is about to take a hit. Which outside linebacker could see their role diminish with the Cowboys wanting to see more from their 2026 first-round pick?

Schottenheimer did share some of the personnel plans, though. The biggest one involves first-round rookie EDGE Malachi Lawrence, and the short version is that he is going to play more. That shouldn’t be a surprise given how Lawrence has been playing.

He got his first sack last week versus the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. His pressure rate of 14.3% in 2026 ranks him fourth among qualified NFL rookies per PFF, behind David Bailey (16.4%), Sonny Styles (15.0%) and Cashius Howell (14.8%).

But the Cowboys’ plans to play him more raise a question I find fascinating: Where are Lawrence’s new snaps coming from?

Brian Schottenheimer OK with Cowboys’ players-only meeting panned by Mike Tomlin – ESPN.com

There has been a lot made of the report that the Cowboys defense had a “players only” meeting earlier this week. The meeting was heavily criticized by former Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin on the “New Heights” podcast, but Brian Schottenheimer seems not concerned with the meeting.

The players-only meeting recently held by the Dallas Cowboys‘ defense has become such a topic around the NFL that even Mike Tomlin weighed in with a concerned response.

But Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer is not pushing the panic button, saying that the meeting doesn’t bother him and that it “means everyone’s rowing in the same direction.”

Dallas star linebacker DeMarvion Overshown revealed Monday that the defensive players held the meeting after last week’s home loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Overshown said the players “went by bullet point, bullet point,” discussing whether they were meeting the team’s various standards.

Cowboys at Packers: Matchups to watch in Week 6 – Brian Martin, Blogging the Boys

After dropping their week five game to the 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Cowboys are in a must-win scenario in week six heading to Green Bay. What are some of the key matchups the Cowboys will need to win, in order to come out with a road victory against a long-time NFC rival?

The Packers are coming off a game in which they held D’Andre Swift to just 43 yards on nine carries and only allowed Chicago to rush for a total of 81 rushing yards. They’ll be hoping to do the same this week against Javonte Williams and the Cowboys. Williams probably has other plans.

He’s been a touchdown scoring machine so far this year with six, but is currently struggling to find consistency as a runner, averaging just 3.7 yards per carry. If Williams has success on the ground, it should sway the game in Dallas’ favor.

item.title: Commanders look to bounce back from a brutal week as they visit 49ers on Monday night
item.description: Hogs Haven looks at key factors that affect this Week 6 Monday Night Football game between the 49ers & Commanders
item.content:encoded:
Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates as we go inside the matchup to get you ready for every opponent the Commanders face in 2026.

From John Portis:

The Washington Commanders enter Week 6 coming off one of the worst clock management gaffes in team history. After tying the Giants this past Sunday, the 1-3-1 Commanders will be looking to get their second win of the season as the team takes on the San Francisco 49ers on Monday Night Football. Back in July, Bill-in-Bangkok predicted a hot start to the season for the Niners but seems to have underestimated their win total, as San Francisco narrowly defeated the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 last week to remain undefeated.

49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan was expected to have one of the best offenses in football, but key injuries to several players, including wide receivers Rickey Pearsall, Demarcus Robinson, Christian Kirk and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling, have limited the team’s potential. News got worse for the Niners last week, as Deebo Samuel was ruled out with a hamstring injury and is expected to miss an extended period of time. Free-agent addition Mike Evans, who is fighting through a rib injury and now Achilles soreness, is playing at a high level and leads the team with 24 receptions for 326 receiving yards and three touchdowns. Quarterback Brock Purdy has made up the difference for the depleted wide receiver corps by playing at an MVP level, and his 85.5 QBR through the first five weeks leads the league. While Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle are starting to slow down, they are still very talented, and the Niners rank 3rd in team offense.

Shanahan’s offense was always expected to be good, but San Francisco’s defense has been the real surprise of the 2026 season. After losing Robert Saleh to the Titans, the 49ers turned to Raheem Morris to coordinate their defense. So far, Morris looks to be an upgrade for them and has improved the team’s performance in multiple defensive categories.

The improvement is even more impressive given the team has been without edge rusher Nick Bosa, a player Shanahan indicated has a chance to return this week, although Dre Greenlaw’s suspension was upheld and the linebacker will miss Monday night’s game. San Francisco has made explosive plays on offense while limiting them on defense, and the 49ers are playing well on both sides of the ball, which is why the team remains undefeated headed into Week 6.

The challenge may seem insurmountable for Washington, but one of the positives from last week is that Jayden Daniels appears to have no limitations following his second left-elbow dislocation. The Commanders’ franchise quarterback was spectacular last Sunday and recorded 199 passing yards with a 68% completion rate, along with 103 rushing yards and 2 TDs on 8 rushes. Running back Bill Croskey-Merritt also demonstrated his explosive potential behind an improved offensive line with a 33-yard touchdown run and another 22-yard rush to set up one of Jayden Daniels’ touchdowns. Bill is dealing with a groin injury but could still sit up Monday night.

Washington’s run defense continues to be ranked in the top 10, and the possible return of Trey Amos and Nick Cross could bolster a secondary that has struggled this season. Both players practiced in full yesterday. Washington’s front seven will need to do a better job of generating pressure against an offensive line that allowed zero sacks through the first four weeks of the season, although Seattle’s defense was able to get home last Sunday, generating 3 sacks and 3 turnovers while limiting the 49ers offense to 269 yards, 14 first downs, and an average of 4.8 yards per play.

The most important component for head coach Dan Quinn and his players will be the belief they can win in Santa Clara on Monday night. Amik Robertson’s early response this week would indicate that they have the needed belief.

Betting Lines

Oddsmakers have established the home team as the solid favorite for this matchup.

  • Point Spread: 49ers -7.5
  • Game Total (Over/Under): 50.5 points

Bill-in-Bangkok’s original preview published July 5th:

Date: October 19, 2026, 8:15 p.m. ET (Monday Night Football)
Location: Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California

The 49ers are off to Australia to open their season by playing Thursday Night Football in Victoria at the historic Melbourne Cricket Ground, where I once watched Day 5 of a test match between South Africa and the Aussies (which Australia won handily).

San Fran then plays 3 home games in a row (presumably as payback for the Australia travel) before a short road trip to Seattle. They return to Levi’s Stadium for the MNF game against Washington — their 4th home game in 5 weeks!

The Niners should have at least a couple of wins on the board as they play the Cardinals and Dolphins in two of those home games (who were ranked 29th & 32nd, respectively, in ESPN’s latest Football Power Index). They may not be above .500, however, since their 3 other games are NFC & AFC West contests against the Rams, Seahawks and Broncos.

We know that Kyle Shanahan always feels a little extra motivation against Washington, where he felt he and his dad got the metaphorical bum’s rush out the door at the end of the 2013 season, the senior Shanahan’s final NFL coaching job after a probable Hall of Fame NFL coaching career.

The All-Time Series Numbers

Dating back to 1952, San Francisco and Washington have played each other 36 times, including 4 playoff games.

The Niners have had the best of both regular season and postseason, winning 3 of the 4 playoff games, and holding onto a commanding 23-12-1 lead overall. Washington’s sole playoff win over the 49ers came in the NFC Championship game after the 1983 season.

Things have been a little less one-sided since 2017, with Washington winning 2 out of 5 regular season games. You may remember the not-so-classic mud bowl played in Landover during monsoon rain in 2019 when the 49ers won 9-0.

The last time Washington beat the 49ers, they were branded as the “Football Team” in the 2020 COVID-affected season. This will be the first meeting between the two teams in the AP/DQ/JD5 era (though not the first of the Josh Harris ownership), so Dan Quinn will be looking to get off on the right foot against his former offensive coordinator — who may have cost Quinn a Super Bowl win with his 4th quarter playcalling against the Patriots on February 5th, 2017.

49ers Coaching Changes

The most notable changes included hiring Raheem Morris as the defensive coordinator and adding former Bears head coach Matt Eberflus assistant head coach/defense

Offense

Klay Kubiak returns as the offensive coordinator in 2026, but a few things should be clear. First and foremost, it is Kyle Shanahan, the head coach, who designs the offense and calls the plays. Just like Kyle is the son of Mike Shanahan, Klay is the son of Gary Kubiak, who played & coached under Mike Shanahan, and younger brother to Klint Kubiak, who is currently the rookie head coach of the Raiders — an unenviable job — and who also lists stops as an offensive coach in Denver and San Francisco on his resume.

This is a multi-generational family affair — involving both the Shanahans and Kubiaks — but in 2026, it is Kyle’s offense, one that he inherited from his dad, but one that he has continued to adapt and refine.

In a sense, an entire swath of NFL offenses are credited as direct or indirect descendants of the Shanahan offense, with Kyle often credited as the progenitor (as opposed to his father, Mike).

Kyle’s continued success in running an offensive scheme that seems to enhance the performance of offensive linemen, quarterbacks and running backs regardless of pedigree belies the idea that a superstar quarterback is a prerequisite for NFL success, as well as the belief that, once opposing defenses get film of your scheme, they’ll find a way to stop it.

The 49ers’ Kubiak/Shanahan offensive scheme relies on a heavy outside-zone running game perfectly matched with mirrored play-action passing concepts. By making running and passing plays look completely identical at the snap, the 49ers ruin defensive eye discipline and create hesitation. The system further stresses opponents by utilizing league-leading rates of pre-snap motion and versatile, positionless players to create structural mismatches. This lethal combination forces defenders to think rather than react, routinely resulting in blown coverages and massive gains.

Defense

Based on what I’ve seen from Raheem Morris over the past few years and what I’ve read about him this offseason, the defensive scheme that he implements with the 49ers will likely integrate a hybrid, multiple-front structure that, like so many other NFL defensive schemes, is designed to elevate post-snap ambiguity. While it should rely on a traditional four-down base defensive alignment, Morris should also incorporate odd-front looks, such as 3-4 and five-man structures, to disguise pressure and confuse offenses.

Within this scheme, Nick Bosa is expected to shift from a rigid wide-9 path to alternate styles where he occasionally stands up or aligns tighter inside, allowing the defense to manufacture isolated matchups and run tactical stunts. This variable look should force opposing blockers to diagnose what’s happening on the fly. It is almost guaranteed that Fred Warner will wear the green dot, tasked with managing the defense.

The secondary structure under Morris transitions away from predictable, stationary coverage shells toward a system heavily reliant on simulated pressures and back-end disguise.

The coverage should rely on cornerback Renardo Green to utilize his physical press-man capabilities on the boundary, disrupting wide receiver route timing right at the line of scrimmage.

By tightening coverage on the perimeter, Morris can simultaneously elevate the team’s blitz rates and manipulate safe-zone depth, leveraging safety Ji’Ayir Brown to mask post-snap rotations and eliminate vertical passing lanes over the deep middle.

This integration of flexible front-seven alignments and aggressive boundary techniques, common to many NFL defenses, aims to keep offensive protection schemes off-balance and force opposing QBs into costly mistakes.

Summary

In ESPN’s recent Power Index, the 49ers were ranked #5 while the Commanders were ranked #21, which indicates that this Week 6 Monday Night Football game won’t be much of a contest, but, as I alluded above, the league’s scheduling of the Commanders in 2026 — 5 prime time games, an international game, 2 late-afternoon NFC East games to open the season (that’s 8 high-profile games out of 14) — indicates that networks and Roger Goodell expect a lot more out of this re-tooled Washington team than do ESPN or the oddsmakers. If the league office and the networks are right, this early-season NFC Monday night matchup could be critical to both teams’ playoff hopes.

Key statistical 2025 rankings

The 49ers will have as much continuity on offense as any team in the league, with no change at head coach and offensive coordinator and limited roster change outside of the wide receiver group. Defensively, the 49ers were ranked in the top half of the league under Robert Saleh, who left to take over as head coach of the Titans. The core defensive roster is back, bolstered by 4 mid-round draft picks and former Cowboy Osa Odighizuwa.

Offensive Rankings

  • Total Offense: Ranked 7th in total yards (5,974 yards).
  • Scoring Offense: Ranked 10th in points scored, averaging 25.7 points per game.
  • Passing Offense: Ranked 5th in passing yards per game, averaging 244.5 yards.
  • Efficiency: Ranked 4th in quick-passing efficiency on first-read throws released under 2.5 seconds.

Defensive Rankings

  • Scoring Defense: Ranked 13th in points allowed, giving up 21.8 points per game.
  • Total Defense: Ranked 20th in total yards allowed per game, yielding 340.2 yards.
  • Yards Allowed: Ranked 13th in overall net defensive yards allowed (5,784 yards).

Roster Moves: Trades, Free Agency, and the Draft

Trades and Free Agency

Player trades

The San Francisco 49ers strengthened their interior DL by acquiring veteran Osa Odighizuwa from the Dallas Cowboys for a 2026 3rd-round draft pick. The 27-year-old DT brings 17 career sacks and five seasons of experience to the Bay Area, and is expected to provide three-down versatility and bolster a run defense that struggled last season.

  • WR Mike Evans

Free agent losses

  • WR Kendrick Bourne
  • WR Jauan Jennings
  • DT Jordan Elliott

The 2026 NFL Draft

Round 2, No. 33: De’Zhaun Stribling (WR, Ole Miss) – A speedy receiver who ran a 4.36-second 40-yard dash.


Round 3, No. 70: Romello Height (EDGE, Texas Tech) – A pass rusher expected to serve as a third-down specialist.

item.title: Bo Nix: I don't know where the disconnect is offensively
item.description: The point of playing football games is to win football games and the Broncos were able to do that against the Seahawks on Thursday night, but the result didn't shield their quarterback Bo Nix from some harsh criticism after the game.
item.content:encoded:
The point of playing football games is to win football games and the Broncos were able to do that against the Seahawks on Thursday night, but the result didn't shield their quarterback Bo Nix from some harsh criticism after the game.

During the Prime Video postgame show, former NFL quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick called Nix's performance in the 17-14 overtime victory "garbage." The Broncos picked up 153 yards on a pair of early touchdown drives that staked them to a 14-0 lead, but they only picked up two first downs over the rest of the night while punting seven times and the futility allowed the Seahawks to send the game to overtime.

Nix finished 17-of-27 for 107 yards and the team's longest pass play went for 16 yards, which he said after the game was not part of a design to be overly conservative and that he doesn't "understand why we can’t really push the ball vertically right now." Nix said he recognizes the need to do that for the offense to pull equal weight to the defense in Denver.

“We’re definitely capable," Nix said. "We’ve shown it and I don’t where the disconnect is right now to be honest with you. . . . I just think we're really, for some reason, struggling to find those explosive plays and that’s what makes an offense really spectacular — finding explosive plays. And right now we don’t have those.”

The one positive that Nix could point to is that the Broncos did not turn the ball over while the Seahawks gave it away three times, including an overtime interception that set up Denver's winning points. Head coach Sean Payton didn't delve into the offense's struggles beyond saying "we’re going to see a lot that we want to clean up," but it is clear that his decision to take over playcalling has not solved all that's wrong with Nix or the rest of the unit.

item.title: Brock Bowers already NFL’s best receiving tight end in football
item.description: The Bills have another elite receiving option to face defensively
item.content:encoded:
The week after they faced arguably the best receiver in football in Puka Nacua, the Buffalo Bills will see the NFL’s best receiving tight on Sunday when they face the Las Vegas Raiders.

That is no slight to Dalton Kincaid, or George Kittle, Trey McBride, Sam LaPorta, or any of the other excellent tight ends in today’s increasingly tight-end happy league.

Brock Bowers is a different beast.

In his first professional season, Bowers caught an NFL rookie record 112 passes. Not just for a tight end. A rookie at any position. And he did so at a remarkable 2.02 yards per route run. It’s not as if the Raiders just funneled him targets to re-write the record books. He was legitimately efficient on his 592 routes and 148 targets that season, as he amassed 1,194 yards — the same yardage figure as CeeDee Lamb that year on only two more targets.

This season, Bowers missed the first two games due to injury.

In the three outings since his return, he has 10 catches for 116 yards and one touchdown on 12 targets, six catches for 86 yards and a score on 11 targets, and eight snags for 110 yards and a touchdown on nine targets.

His yards per route run figure of 2.79 is tops in the NFL among tight ends.

And he aligns everywhere, so he’s not a tight end by the classic definition.

Entering this game, Bowers has run routes from the outside 40.1% of the time, the highest rate among all qualifying tight ends. It’s almost identical to the percentage at which Zay Flowers has run his routes on the outside.

While certainly not the largest, nor most physical imposing tight end in the league, Bowers has maintained ridiculous reliability in traffic. He had a 53.3% contested-catch rate as a rookie. Then it was an outstanding 65.2% a season ago, and he’s 7-of-10 in those scenarios this season entering this contest.

He’s not a huge tackle-breaker — only nine thus far in his NFL career. He gets open. He catches everything.

Kirk Cousins has a 136.5 rating when targeting Bowers in his three games. And the tight end leads Las Vegas in all receiving categories.

In a game after the Bills saw Puka earn 24 targets and catch 17 of them — albeit at a very minimal 8.1 yards per catch — Buffalo’s defense could be in for another individually high-volume, funnel-the-offense-through-one-player type of outing if they don’t specifically make it a top priority to limit Bowers in this game.

item.title: Does Samaje Perine deserve a larger role at running back over Chase Brown?
item.description: Perine led the Bengals in rushing against Miami. Was it a sign of things to come?
item.content:encoded:
Samaje Perine was the Cincinnati Bengals’ leading rusher on Sunday against the Miami Dolphins, and he provided a spark that this ground game hasn’t had enough of so far this year.

The veteran running back logged 14 carries for 68 yards during the game. That 4.9 yards per carry is the highest number for a Bengals running back this season. Perine also added 2 receptions for 10 yards, and found the end zone for Joe Burrow’s second touchdown pass of the game.

Chase Brown has not been able to get fully going consistently this year in the running game. He had 20 carries for 80 yards against Houston, and followed that up with a respectable 13 carries for 61 yards in Pittsburgh. Against Jacksonville in Week 4, he only ran the ball 9 times for a total of 10 yards. This week he ran the ball 13 times for 39 yards.

One thing I still like about what Brown brings to the table is being a receiving threat out of the backfield for the Bengals. He hauled in three receptions for 21 yards against the Dolphins. One of those came on a play with Perine in the backfield, and a play-action fake to get Brown the ball out in the flat. He was able to make a guy miss and picked up the first down.

Perine, on the other hand, is never going to wow anyone with his speed or elusiveness (except for the Chiefs in the 2021-22 AFC Championship), but he is a dependable player who consistently moves the chains when given opportunities. His 14 carries on Sunday actually outnumbered the 13 carries he had during the first four games of the season.

I think getting the two players closer to a 60-40 split on carries each game makes sense going forward. With that split, you can afford to give either guy closer to the 60% based on who has the hotter hand during that particular game.

Do you think Samaje Perine deserves a larger role in the offense moving forward? Sound off in the comments.

item.title: A.J. Brown brings ‘fresh juice’ to Patriots offense
item.description: The wide receiver returned to practice earlier this week.
item.content:encoded:
After spending the designated four weeks on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain he suffered in Week 1, New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown has been cleared for practice. He did not participate fully on Wednesday or Thursday, though, making his status for Sunday against the New York Jets uncertain.

Still, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels noted how it was “good to see him back out on the practice field,” and that Brown returning could provide a “fresh juice” to the guys in the wide out room.

“This happens quite a bit for us,” he said. “You miss a guy for a week, two weeks, sometimes longer than that, and then you have an opportunity to get him back during the course of the season, it’s always good. It brings some fresh juice to the guys and to the unit. We know what he can do when he’s out there and he’s healthy. We’ll see how the rest of this week goes and ultimately what ends up happening.”

The Patriots have gotten inconsistent production from the top of the receiver group in Brown’s absence. This may be partly because there isn’t a weapon that demands extra attention or has the same presence as him.

Since Brown hasn’t played much this season, McDaniels doesn’t have much data to describe how the offense changes with him in it. But he compared it to the way Stefon Diggs drew attention in 2025 against the Jets.

“Last year they doubled Diggs in the Jet game a couple times,” said McDaniels. “So, anytime they put two people on one person, then someone else has a single opportunity.”

As good as it would be for Drake Maye and the New England offense to get their top target back as soon as this Sunday, it was made clear that it was no guarantee from the Patriots’ medical team. McDaniels was asked about having Brown back, which he quickly corrected to “when” they get him back, definitively showing that there is still an argument that Brown is not ready to go yet.

Brown himself said that his status is “still up in the air” and that it is “a coach Vrabel decision” on if he steps on the field for the first time since the third quarter of the season opener against Seattle.

item.title: 8 Things we learned from the Broncos 17-14 OT win over Seattle
item.description: As is becoming customary, the Broncos found a way to win a close game. This time in overtime against Seattle at home.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, Broncos Country!

Another week, another stress-inducing game for the Denver Broncos.

It wasn’t pretty, especially in the second half for Bo Nix and the Denver offense. But the team gritted out another win.

All that matters is the Broncos beat the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks 17-14 in overtime.

Denver now sits at 4-2 after a brutal six-game stretch to start the season. Now the Broncos get a mini-bye before heading to the desert to face the Arizona Cardinals.

Wil Lutz with the clutch kick

You always hold your breath when the Denver kicker attempts a field goal. And all of Broncos Country did that at the end of the game.

Thankfully, it was an exhale of celebration after Lutz nailed the game-winning 53-yard field goal.

On this day, he was big nuts Lutz, and absolutely clutch Lutz. Helluva kick.

Give Denver’s defense its flowers

Down the best cornerback in the NFL in Patrick Surtain II, the team’s best safety in Talanoa Hufanga, and the Broncos hold Jaxon Smith-Njigba and the Seattle offense to 14 points? Damn impressive showing by Denver’s defense.

On top of that, the Broncos forced three turnovers, got five sacks, five tackles for loss, and nine passes defended. Perhaps the stat of the night, Denver got 17 quarterback hits on Sam Darnold.

In a defensive battle, the Broncos outshone one of the best defenses in the league.

The Broncos secondary was fantastic

Without the two best players in the unit, and Riley Moss limited most of the night, Denver’s secondary played an unreal game.

Yes, JSN got his yards, but when the Broncos needed a play, the guys stepped up. Two of the biggest plays coming from Kris Abrams-Draine and Ja’Quan McMillian forcing huge turnovers, the latter getting the game-winning interception. McMillian is making a habit of this for Denver in clutch moments. He also got a sack.

McMillian finished with five tackles (five sol0), one sack, one tackle for loss, two passes defended, and one quarterback hit.

Abrams-Draine had six tackles (four solo) and three passes defended.

All without PSs and Hufanga.

Bo Nix must get better

What we saw from the Broncos quarterback in the second half will not cut it. He must play better. What’s perplexing is how good the offense looked on back-to-back touchdown drives in the first half.

Why does it have to be one or the other?

Obviously, some of the credit goes to the Seattle defense. The Seahawks rank at the top or near the top for each statistical category. But Nix is going to have to start playing with more consistency because what he’s putting on the field is not good enough.

It no doubt helps to sit at 4-2, having faced five of the best teams in the NFL, but figure it out.

Denver’s running game is terrible

The Broncos finished with 74 yards rushing on Thursday night. How the heck did they get that many?

I don’t know if it’s J.K. Dobbins or the offensive line suddenly being terrible at run blocking, but this is bad. Perhaps rookie Jonah Coleman is the savior, and he’ll be back in Week 7 against the Cardinals.

But similar to Nix, the running game issues have to get fixed. It’s brutal to watch Denver attempt to run the football right now.

Dominance at home continues

The Mile High Magic has returned. The Broncos improved to 3-0 at home this season after going 9-2 if you include the postseason.

Denver has always been one of the best, if not the best, home-field advantages in the NFL. To see the success at home return like this is great to see.

Throwback jerseys shine again

There is no better throwback jersey in the NFL than the Broncos. And to have Seattle rock their throwbacks gave us veteran fans flashbacks to the old AFC West days.

Just like at home, the Broncos remain unbeaten when they rock the snot rocket.

Sitting at 4-2 is quite the feat

As noted at the top, Denver just faced a brutal six-game stretch to start the season, and they sit at 4-2.

When the schedule was released, every single person in Broncos Country would take that record.

What should give fans hope is that the Broncos haven’t played their best yet. Similar to last season, we didn’t see the team start putting it all together until the calendar turned to November.

Yet despite ugly games and performances, Nix and the offense being a disaster, they’ve beaten four of the best teams in football.

That’s reason enough to feel good about this team.

item.title: NFL predictions: Falcons must win trenches against the Bears
item.description: The Falcons face the Bears in Week 6. How will Atlanta fare against Chicago’s high-octane offense with Caleb Williams returning?
item.content:encoded:
The Falcons fell to the Ravens in overtime on Sunday Night Football in Week 5, breaking a two-game winning streak where the offense averaged a blazing 40 points per game. Atlanta came back down to earth against an injured but still extremely well-coached Baltimore team, falling to 2-3 with the most difficult stretch of the schedule still to come. It’s a disappointing result for the Falcons, but hopefully a learning experience for the new coaching staff.

Attention now shifts to Week 6’s matchup with the Bears, who possess one of the league’s most fearsome offenses. Chicago is the only team in the NFL that has rushed for more yards than Atlanta, and should see starting quarterback Caleb Williams return to the lineup after a three-week absence. This is likely to be the toughest test yet for the Falcons defense, who are very shorthanded at cornerback and edge rusher. Unlike the Ravens, however, the Bears defense is quite vulnerable to both the run and pass.

Despite Williams’ return and the Bears offensive prowess, the Falcons are just 1.5-point home underdogs in Week 6. The over/under of 51.5 suggests an offensive showcase, and Atlanta is going to need to put up points and control the clock to keep pace with Chicago.

Falcons vs Bears Week 6 predictions

This matchup presents a major opportunity for the Falcons to step up and win the trenches on both sides of the ball—similar to how they dominated both the Packers and Saints earlier in the season. The Bears have a good offensive line, but are likely to be missing bruising running back Kyle Monangai for the game. D’Andre Swift is a good runner himself, but Chicago has been most effective with the two-headed attack of Swift and Monangai—who is responsible for nearly as many yards and TDs as Swift. Caleb Williams will also factor in as a runner, but there’s no telling how he’ll perform in his first game back from injury.

On the other side of the ball, the Bears will be without top edge rusher Montez Sweat due to a PED suspension. Veteran Dayo Odeyingbo is also in danger of missing the game with a quad injury. At linebacker, starter T.J. Edwards and reserve Keyshaun Elliott also missed practice for most of the week. That’s a lot of injuries piling up the in front seven against a Falcons team who would love nothing more than to run the ball. While former Falcons Grady Jarrett and Kentavius Street are performing well as pass rushers, neither has been an impact run defender.

If Atlanta’s offensive line can bounce back and dominate the way they did back in Weeks 3 and 4, that’s a pathway to success for the Falcons. We all know this offense is a lot better when Bijan and Brian Robinson and getting chunk yardage on the ground, and that’ll be the most important thing to establish early in the game. Long sustained drives will also help keep Chicago’s offense off the field and the defense fresher over the long haul.

On defense, this is another big test for a Falcons front that got beat up by the Ravens. I think Atlanta can get pressure, but they’ll have to also play disciplined football against the rushing threat of Caleb Williams. I’d expect a different approach this week than what we saw against Baltimore, perhaps with a QB spy involved on the majority of plays. It’ll be significantly easier to defend just D’Andre Swift versus Swift and Monangai, so that could also be a boon for the Falcons.

At the end of the day, Atlanta’s depleted secondary presents some issues. I expect the Bears to have success in the passing game, and that means this could turn into a shootout. In that scenario, it’ll be hard for the Falcons to keep pace with Chicago. This will be the offense’s biggest test yet, as it might require a more pass-heavy approach from Penix throughout the game.

All that being said, I think the Bears with Caleb Williams at the helm are possibly the most dangerous offense in football. Atlanta goes back and forth with Chicago throughout the game, but the defense can’t stop Chicago enough thanks to their secondary injuries. The Falcons fall to Chicago, 31-27, but do show some really nice things in the process.
