This week’s opponent could bring a different approach as the Giants take on the New Orleans Saints on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, Fox). Wilson’s track record doesn’t show a heavy lean on the blitz. His Titans defense blitzed just 22.8% of dropbacks over the previous two seasons, the 22nd-highest rate. He sent DB blitzes 9.3% of dropbacks, which was 25th over that span. Perhaps that changes a bit with the Giants short-handed on pass rushers. It might be the best way for them to survive.

Giants embracing the underdog role

Giants adamant Kayvon Thibodeaux is making a bigger impact than modest stats indicate | New York Post

Sunday was almost a homecoming game for Kayvon Thibodeaux.  The Saints called the Giants about trading for Thibodeaux during April’s draft but found the asking price — believed to be a third-round pick — too high. 

Watching from afar as reports surfaced, including from The Post, Thibodeaux posted an image from “Fast & Furious” to social media with the tagline, “You thought you could leave without saying goodbye.” 

Jameis Winston’s starting dream is alive as the Giants roll into a game against the Saints | FOX Sports

When Jameis Winston signed with the New Orleans Saints in 2020 initially to back up Drew Brees and then to be in the mix to succeed him at quarterback, he was long removed from winning the Heisman Trophy in college and being the top pick in the draft.

He did not give up on being a starter in the NFL again, like he was early in his career with Tampa Bay. “I dreamt of it,” Winston said. “And now it’s here.”

Giants WR reveals details of intense exchange with Jameis Winston: ‘You know how to read lips?’ | NJ.com

Winston wanted Mooney to flush the drop and refocus — echoing what Mooney had told Winston in the wake of his own mistakes. Said Mooney: “That was his opportunity to tell me, ‘As much as you tell me to f— it, this is my time to tell you: F— it. It’s OK. Just move on. I’m coming back to you right now.’”

It wasn’t just the drop that had Mooney annoyed in that moment when it appeared he was rolling his eyes at Winston. In reality, Mooney said, he was aggravated about how the afternoon had unfolded. “It was just how the game was going for me,” he said. “I got face masked. I got poked in the eye. When I had a ball, I got ran into, and I thought it was a [pass interference]. It’s just that things weren’t going well for me.”

‘Big, fast, physical’ Giants tight end emerges as special teams playmaker | The Record

Theo Johnson entered the NFL harboring dreams of becoming one of the league’s top tight ends. The former New York Giants coaching staff used to show him highlights of Rob Gronkowski, pulling him out of meetings to bring him upstairs, just to break down Gronkowski video for inspiration and motivation.

Now in his third season, Johnson isn’t giving up on that goal just yet.

Confident Giants kicker Dominic Zvada: ‘If nothing has changed, nothing should change’ | New York Daily News

Zvada said he spent Monday dissecting what went wrong and now has no need for a rear-view mirror as he prepares for the New Orleans Saints. A return to MetLife Stadium and to a turf field might help his footing, and he is no less confident than he was last week.

“I really just try and focus on what I can control,” he said. “That’s kind of how I’ve been able to have success early in the season is by just focusing on not the score or where we’re at in the game or anything like that. It’s just focused on going out there, having that mental checklist in my head and lining up and kicking the ball through the uprights. That’s really all I need to focus on. I’m kind of just forcing myself to focus on that, and when you force yourself to focus on that, everything else just kind of fades out. And then you’re just kind of in your own world. So it’s nice.”

New York Giants’ John Harbaugh: Isaiah Likely a ‘unique kind of athlete’ | USAToday.com

“When he was being evaluated, he went in the fourth round; I think it was late fourth round. Nobody really could get their arms around him. He made all these plays in college, but it just looked different. You see it out here, it turns out it’s really good what he does,” Harbaugh said. “He’s elusive; he can get away in man and zone coverage. He’s got a great feel; he’s got great hands, he has an amazing catch radius. He’s an elusive runner, a good, strong runner. So, all those things that are football. He’s also, and this was in college, he was crazy good as a perimeter blocker. He would launch guys through the air, like five yards through the air sometimes at Coastal. He’s a really good perimeter blocker here too. He’s translated really well, and I think he’s been able to really express that here this year. The kind of player he is, and it’s just great to see.”

item.title: Broncos won despite totaling just 32 yards on their last 10 possessions
item.description: The Broncos' offense was stunningly bad for most of Thursday night's game.
item.content:encoded:
The Broncos' offense was stunningly bad for most of Thursday night's game. They beat the Seahawks anyway.

Over Denver's final 10 possessions — two in the second quarter, three in the third quarter, four in the fourth quarter and one in overtime — the Broncos' offense totaled 32 yards. Seven of those 10 possessions ended in punts, two ended with the ends of the first and second halves, and the one in overtime began in field goal range and ended with the game-winning field goal.

Broncos quarterback Bo Nix could not move the offense at all: He threw the ball 27 times for 107 yards, got sacked twice for a loss of 13 yards, and had four rushes for two yards. Add all that up, and in 33 plays, Nix totaled 96 yards. That's 2.9 yards per play. Usually, you can't win in the NFL when your quarterback is playing like that.

Fortunately for the Broncos, Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold also played a losing game. Darnold's overtime interception did something Nix couldn't: Put the Broncos in position to win.

A big development in the AI space is that neurons are now legible. I’m so grateful we have the football version of Leonardo Da Vinci coaching my favorite football team. I’m even more grateful that the Denver Broncos beat the Seattle Seahawks.  

49ers’ Christian McCaffrey is working less. His thoughts? It’s complicated (paywall)
“I want to win — whatever it takes to win games,” McCaffrey said. “I think what I love about this team is you’ve got a bunch of selfish, unselfish guys. Obviously, people want the ball every play, but not at the expense of the team. …

“I think we’ve got to do whatever it takes to win and when you have a roster like ours where the ball can get spread around so much, you should probably not get as many touches, either. It’s never my job to count them, but to make them count.”

Why is Shanahan finally taking better care of McCaffrey this season? It’s not about extending his career. It’s about reinvigorating his rushing attack.”

Mike Evans broke ribs and got even better: How the 49ers WR’s history made him who he is (paywall)
“But over time, his skills sharpened, and he became a sort of point forward — someone who could bring the ball up the court, guard the opponent’s tallest player and finish with 16 rebounds.

He plays wide receiver like a rebounder, using his tremendous length — the 6-foot-5 Evans has a nearly 7-foot wingspan — to box out defensive backs when the ball is in the air. The quarterback’s rule when targeting Evans: Even when he’s not open, he’s open.

“It’s feel, and it’s years of repetition,” Evans said of knowing where a defender is even when he’s behind him. “That helps a lot.”

Terry Petteway also learned how to tap into his pupil’s hypercompetitiveness. He’d point to the biggest kid on the other squad and tell Mike he couldn’t guard him.

“He’d look over and say, ‘What? That guy?’” Terry recalled. “Then he’d go and tear the guy’s head off. All you needed to do to motivate Mike was tell him he couldn’t do something.”

Asked whether Evans ever got into fights on the court or football field, Terry laughed. “That’s not a fair question!” he protested. “I’m gonna put it this way: Mike was never, ever going to back down from anybody. And he’s still like that today.”

Christian Kirk getting closer to making a difference for injury-riddled 49ers
“I believe I have a lot of really good football left,” Kirk said on Thursday. “In no way, shape or form, I thought about anything other than that. It’s just all about working to get my body back to feeling great, to be able to go out and play.”

Kawakami: John Lynch’s near-perfect offseason has relaunched this 49ers era (paywall)
“I’ve already said that Odighizuwa is better than Hargrave. Let’s go bigger than that with this rookie: Halton’s Seahawks-wrecking performance last Sunday was the 49ers’ best game by a defensive tackle since DeForest Buckner in his prime.

And Halton is only 22.

It’s early. But Halton, the 107th pick in this draft, looks like he’s everything the 49ers hoped to get when they signed Hargrave or took Alfred Collins 43rd in 2025 and Javon Kinlaw 14th in 2020.

The minor complication is that Halton looks like a natural three-technique DT. And you usually play only one of those at a time, with a nose-tackle type next to him on early downs. item.title: Eagles-Panthers matchups to watch in Week 6
item.description: Here are some key matchups to watch as the Eagles host the Carolina Panthers in Week 6.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles-Panthers matchups to watch in Week 6 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Eagles (2-3) return home to host the Carolina Panthers (2-2) at Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday.

Let’s get to the matchups:

Eagles run D vs. Chuba Hubbard

The Panthers have a middle-of-the-pack rushing offense led by lead back Chuba Hubbard. In four games this year, Hubbard has 306 yards and 3 touchdowns on 61 carries for an average of 5.0 yards per carry. The Panthers also have former Eagle AJ Dillon, who has 43 yards on 17 carries and hasn’t been very involved and has missed practice this week. But Hubbard is pretty good. He went for nearly 1,200 yards a couple seasons ago and is off to a nice start in 2026.

In just four games, Hubbard is seventh in the NFL with 78 rushing yards over expected. The only players ahead of him are Kenneth Walker III, Bijan Robinson, Jaylen Warren, James Cook, Jayden Daniels and Bucky Irving. He is also averaging 3.4 rushing yards after contact per attempt, with ranks sixth in the NFL. So it’ll be important for the Eagles’ defense to get him down. That starts up front with Jordan Davis, Jalen Carter and Co. but the linebackers will be a big part of that too. Zack Baun has been really good all season but we expect to see a rotation between Jihaad Campbell and Jeremiah Trotter Jr. for that other spot.

Eagles corners vs. Tetairoa McMillan

The Eagles used the No. 8 overall pick to select McMillan last spring and the 23-year-old is off to a great start in his second NFL season. Before the Panthers’ bye week, McMillan had a monster game in a win over the Lions with 14 catches for 192 yards and 2 touchdowns. McMillan is 10th in the NFL in receiving with 385 yards and has played just four games, while most of the guys above him have already played five games. He’s averaging over 96 yards per game.

McMillan has played 75.9% of his snaps on the outside this season but will line up in the slot on occasion. The Eagles feel very good about their cornerbacks this season with Quinyon Mitchell and Riq Woolen outside and Cooper DeJean in the slot. Mitchell has been outstanding but he hasn’t been traveling with opposing receivers because the Eagles seem to really trust Woolen on the other side. While McMillan leads the Panthers in receiving, Jalen Coker is second with 18 catches for 222 yards and a couple touchdowns. Coker plays both out wide and in the slot and really seems to thrive against zone coverage.

Eagles DL vs. Panthers OL

The Panthers have given up just 10 sacks in four games but have given up a pressure rate of 42.7%, per NextGen Stats. That ranks as the fifth-worst percentage in the NFL. The Panthers were without starting left guard Damien Lewis before the bye week and he has been limited this week with an elbow injury. Second-year UDFA Corey Bullock started in Week 4 and gave up three pressures and a sack. So keep an eye if it’s Bullock against Moro Ojomo and Jordan Davis, especially if Jalen Carter gets doubled on the other side. Carter is coming off his best game of the season and could have another big one on Sunday against this interior.

Here’s a look at the Panthers’ projected line and how much pressure they have surrendered this season:

LT Rasheed Walker: 20 pressures, 5 hits, 1 sack
LG Corey Bullock: 4 pressures, 0 hits, 1 sack
C Luke Fortner: 15 pressures, 2 hits, 1 sack
RG Robert Hunt: 12 pressures, 1 hit
RT Monroe Freeling: 15 pressures, 3 hits, 2 sacks

It’s worth noting that the rookie Feeling missed practice to start the week with a knee injury but was limited on Thursday. It’s possible we see either Taylor Moton or Stone Forsythe at right tackle in this game.

Vic Fangio vs. Bryce Young

You know Vic Fangio well enough by now to know he doesn’t just pass around compliments. And he was very complimentary of Bryce Young this week.

“The quarterback has really progressed,” Fangio said. “I think I coached against him when he was a rookie, and to see the progress that he’s made from then to now, kudos to him and their coaching staff. He is a really good processor, makes quick decisions, knows where to go with the ball. He’s elusive, he’s a scrambler, really good anticipation. Very, very impressed by him.”

Young, 25, was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 draft and took some time to develop. He’s off to a great start in 2026. He has completed 62.3% of his passes for 1,268 yards with 9 touchdowns and 2 interceptions in four games with a passer rating of exactly 100.0. Young doesn’t have a bunch of yards rushing this year — just 19 in four games — but he is elusive and will use his legs to buy time to throw downfield.

Tanner McKee vs. Panthers defense

The Eagles will be without Jalen Hurts this week because of a superficial blood clot in his calf. Hurts was ruled out on Thursday after being a full participant in Wednesday’s practice. So Tanner McKee will start after just two days of practice as the QB1. And if you remember, McKee didn’t even enter the year as the Eagles’ backup quarterback. They gave that job to Andy Dalton, who was demoted after throwing an interception in Chicago and was then subsequently released.

McKee, 26, has appeared in six career games with two starts. He has completed 61.4% of his passes for 597 yards with 5 touchdowns and 1 interception. 

This Panthers defense is No. 26 in points allowed and 29th in yards this season. They have been susceptible through the air, so perhaps McKee is able to find some success.

Markel Bell vs. Jaelan Phillips

The Eagles traded for Jaelan Phillips during last season and wanted to keep him in March before the Panthers went over their walk-away number. The Panthers gave Phillips a deal worth $120 million over four years. And Phillips has played well so far this season for Carolina with two sacks and 14 pressures in four games. Phillips is coming off a hamstring injury so we’ll see if he’s able to play and how effective he is. Phillips primarily lines up on the defensive left, which sets up a matchup against rookie right tackle Markel Bell, who has replaced Lane Johnson. Bell was thrust into action against the Rams a couple weeks ago but got better in Week 5 when he had a full week to prepare. Here’s a look at his pass pro production in his two starts.

Week 4: 34 pass blocking snaps, 6 pressures, 3 sacks
Week 5: 46 pass blocking snaps, 1 pressure

Dameon Pierce vs. improving run D

While the Panthers gave up 400 passing yards in their Week 4 win over the Lions, they limited them to 46 yards on the ground. And they have been getting better each week against the run:

Week 1 vs. CHI: 291 yards
Week 2 at ATL: 157 yards
Week 3 at CLE: 132 yards
Week 4 vs. DET: 46 yards

That 291-yard game allowed to the Bears has really skewed the numbers early in the season but the Panthers are allowing 156.5 yards per game on the ground, which is the second-highest total in the NFL behind just the Cowboys at 168.4. When asked about the Panthers’ defense this week, the first guy Nick Sirianni mentioned was No. 95 (Derrick Brown). Brown, 28, is a seven-year NFL veteran and a Pro Bowler back in 2023.

It looks like the Eagles will be without Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby and Will Shipley this week. So Dameon Pierce is the next man up. Pierce had 14 yards on 11 carries in London.

item.title: Why Eagles players think Tanner McKee is ready for this moment
item.description: Without Jalen Hurts on Sunday, it'll be Tanner McKee under center for the Eagles. His teammates think he's ready.
item.content:encoded:
Why Eagles players think Tanner McKee is ready for this moment originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

A weird Eagles season took another unexpected turn on Thursday when we learned Jalen Hurts is out for Week 6 against the Panthers with a blood clot in his calf.

All of a sudden, Tanner McKee is a starter

“I think everybody’s got a lot of belief in Tanner,” tight end Dallas Goedert said. “When his number has been called upon, he has stepped in and done a good job for us. Obviously, you hate to lose Jalen like that, the leader of the offense. But it’s kind of what we’ve been dealing with all year. The next man has to step up.”

Had Hurts missed one of the first three weeks of this season, it would not have been McKee in there for him. McKee lost a training camp battle to Andy Dalton to be the Eagles’ backup quarterback this season but finally took that job after Dalton threw an ugly interception on the goal line in Chicago in Week 3.

McKee, 26, has been the Eagles’ backup the last couple weeks and Dalton has subsequently been released.

It’s not like the Eagles don’t know anything about McKee. They drafted him in the sixth round of the 2023 season and this is his fourth season with the team. While he has played in just 6 games with 2 starts, McKee has performed well at times. He’s not Hurts, but his teammates have faith in McKee.

“Love everything about him,” left tackle Jordan Mailata said. “His poise, his energy too. High energy guy. It’s not Jalen, where Jalen is cool, calm and collected 24/7. I think Tanner has a very calm nature about him but is also high energy with the way he attacks practice.”

Because the Eagles have suffered so many injuries this season, McKee will actually be out there on Sunday with plenty of second and third-team players — a lot of the guys he spent most of training camp working with. 

On one hand, that’s not great because there’s an obvious lack of talent. On the other, at least there’s going to be some familiarity.

“Tanner is ready,” receiver Darius Cooper said. “He’s a great quarterback, man. Happy to have gotten a lot of time with him last year, over the summer, things of that nature. I feel like he’s ready to go.

“He’s just very poised. And I think that he gets through his progressions very well. And you better be ready when the ball comes because it hits you right in your face.”

McKee (6-6, 231) seemed to outplay Dalton for much of the summer, so it was a bit of a surprise when they pushed him down the depth chart to be their No. 3 to start the season. But McKee definitely has arm talent and he has poise too.

A few of his teammates on Thursday mentioned McKee’s poise. That should come in handy this week with just two days as the QB1 in practice before making his third-career start and his first start that isn’t coming in a Week 18.

“Tanner’s sharp, man,” receiver Elijah Moore said. “He seems as though he’s always ready for the moment. I would say some of his strengths to me that he’s showed is his mental focus. When you see him out at practice, he’s always going through the plays even though he’s not in the position to play. There’s a lot to be excited about with him.”

Goedert said he and McKee got a chance to work together this offseason at a session orchestrated by Hurts and feels pretty comfortable caching passes from him. There might also be a time this week where they’ll try to get in a few extra reps between periods just to make sure they’re on the same page

“I’m just trying to be there for him,” Goedert said. “We had I think one game that we played together. We had a connection going early. Just rely on that and try to win for him, be open for him when he needs me.”

item.title: ‘Ready at a moment's notice': Tanner McKee up for biggest start of his career
item.description: Tanner McKee will make his third career start Sunday, stepping in for Jalen Hurts against the Panthers.
item.content:encoded:
‘Ready at a moment's notice': Tanner McKee up for biggest start of his career originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Tanner McKee has started two games in his NFL career and both were on the last day of the season with mostly backups playing.

So he should feel right at home.

This time, the backups will be playing out of necessity, not because the Eagles have a playoff berth locked up.

McKee, who was the Eagles’ 3rd-stringer until 12 days ago, will make his third NFL start Sunday against the Panthers at the Linc while Jalen Hurts is out with blood clots.

It will be the first meaningful start of his four-year career.

McKee was the Eagles’ 3rd-stringer behind Hurts and Andy Dalton until the Rams game, when Nick Sirianni flip-flopped Dalton and McKee, making McKee No. 2 and Dalton No. 3. The Eagles then released Dalton last Friday, and rookie 5th-round pick Cole Payton became No. 3 behind Hurts and McKee. Dalton threw one pass this year against the Bears and it was picked off. As of now, Payton is No. 2.

McKee’s initial reaction to the news? Concern for his teammate of four years.

“Initially, just hoping the best for him,” McKee said at his locker after practice Wednesday. “Obviously, some things are bigger than football, and his health is obviously that. So hoping that gets taken care of. And we have great doctors here that are going to do everything that they can. So, yeah, I think that was the first thing just making sure he’s OK for that.

“He’s an unbelievable teammate, expressed a lot of confidence in me and just said he’s going to have my back if I need anything. He’s been a great resource for me every game that we’ve been together for the last four years, and he’s going to continue to be that.

“I love Jalen, he’s a great teammate to me, he’s been a great mentor to me. We’ve been brothers for the last four years, and so obviously hope all the best for him.”

The Eagles players found out Hurts was out when they took the field Thursday for their walkthrough and McKee was running the offense.

McKee had to quickly switch gears from concern for Hurts to leading the offense in his place. 

“You’re walking out to walkthrough, and it was like, ‘OK, well, I’m taking the one reps now, and you know, let’s move like I’m going to be the guy,’” he said. “As a backup quarterback, that’s the mindset you have to have. At any moment, you (might have to) be ready to play. On Sunday, it could be the first play, it could be the last play, you have to be ready.

“So it’s kind of a luxury for me to be able to have a few days of getting the ones in practice, getting those reps, and just running the meetings or whatever it is. It’s kind of a luxury for me as a backup to be able to have a week to prepare like that.”

McKee, a 6th-round pick in 2023, beat the Giants on the last day of the 2024 season and lost to the Commanders on the last day of the 2025 season. He’s thrown five touchdown passes and one interception in parts of four games, completing 61 percent of his passes and compiling a 95.7 passer rating.

When McKee beat the Giants in 2024, he became the first Eagles quarterback drafted in the sixth round or later to win a regular-season start since 7th-round pick Koy Detmer beat the 49ers in San Francisco late in the 2002 season (with late-game relief from A.J. Feeley).

McKee and his former Eagles teammate Marcus Mariota are the only quarterbacks in NFL history to throw two touchdowns and no interceptions in each of their first two NFL games. 

It’s not common for a quarterback to go from 3rd string to 2nd string to starter, but that’s where McKee is. He competed with Dalton for the starting job all summer, only to watch Dalton – incorrectly – named Hurts’ backup. But after Dalton’s damaging interception vs. the Bears, McKee moved up to No. 2.

It’s been a weird few weeks, but as a backup QB in the NFL you have to always be ready for anything.

“That’s the NFL,” McKee said. “As a quarterback, especially as a backup quarterback, you have to be ready at a moment’s notice. And so the thing that’s been nice is the way I prepare and the way that I’ve been preparing is not going to change. And so I feel like these last few weeks, whether it was a three, the two, the one, whatever it was, the preparation is going to be the same. 

“I feel like I was ready at any moment the last few weeks. And so now I’m obviously going to be ready this week as well.”

item.title: Winners and Losers from Seahawks vs. Broncos: Benching Sam Darnold must be considered
item.description: The Seahawks are in big trouble for not just a Super Bowl repeat, but returning to the playoffs.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks have a great defense and a mediocre football team right now.

After an ugly 17-14 overtime loss to the Denver Broncos, Seattle sits at 3-3 and are almost certainly going to be only competing for a Wild Card berth. At this rate, missing the playoffs seems distinctly possible if not probable. An offense this bad can sink a season just as much as a great offense can be undone when a defense is rancid.

This is about as clear-cut as a Winners and Losers as you’re going to get, so sit tight.

Seattle Seahawks Winners

Jaxon Smith-Njigba is playing through pain and playing his ass off

Another 12 catches for 134 yards for the NFL’s premier receiver. Without him, Seattle’s offense may be threatening 1992 levels of ineptitude. JSN is not 100 percent and took some huge hits all night, making me wonder if he was going to make it through the game. His toughness is criminally underrated and his strength at the catch point is terrific.

Seattle’s defense didn’t deserve that loss

Okay, the second quarter was bad. Screen passes and short throws and that Devon Witherspoon DPI resulted in two touchdowns allowed back-to-back. Tell me what more the defense could’ve done. Get a turnover? Didn’t have one but they limited Denver to 168 yards of offense and basically nothing after halftime. I thought Tyrice Knight in particular did a great job filling in for Drake Thomas, while Nick Emmanwori continues to look more like himself after his ankle surgery.

There’s very little to complain about outside of (again) the continued lack of consistent pressure from the edge group. The Broncos offense had two good drives out of 11 real attempts to score and it’s unreasonable to expect a defense to play much better than that. If your offense can’t score 15 points minimum to win a game in regulation then that’s on the offense.

George Holani redeems himself for a couple of plays

Hey, he didn’t fumble and got a career-long 13-yard run which set up an angry run touchdown on the next play. After last week’s disaster at least he did something positive and got Seattle’s only TD of the night.

Irv Charles showed more on one kickoff coverage rep

Yes, Denver scored a touchdown anyway, but to see Irv immediately wrap up a returner at the 25 was a breath of fresh air after repeatedly seeing kickoffs go beyond the 30. More Irv! This is what you do!

Seattle Seahawks Losers

Sam Darnold is playing bench-worthy football, there I said it

I defended Darnold from the idea of getting benched last week but left the door open a little bit if it persisted. I’ll preface this by saying that Drew Lock not throwing any picks in his two games is not indicative of a QB who is suddenly not turnover prone anymore. Lock has had plenty of games where he’s looked like a very good starter and then the following week looks like a mess. Playing an awful Arizona Cardinals defense (in which Seattle actually had a good running game to lean on) doesn’t tell me much about how he’d do against way better teams.

But Drew Lock as a backup seemingly has it ingrained in his head not to be reckless with the ball. Sam Darnold is reverting to every bad habit he’s ever had in college and in the NFL, except there is no great payoff like we’ve seen over the past two seasons. Darnold’s NFC Championship Game performance is the single greatest performance by any Seahawks QB in the playoffs and I’ll say that with confidence… but he’s also vying to be a long-term starter and not a mid-level contract guy. You can’t pay him top-level money so that’s out the window, but can you even start him at this rate?

Not everything falls on Sam. This offensive line is not playing well, the running game is mediocre, and Brian Fleury’s pure progression concepts are causing way too many route spacing issues. But Fleury isn’t making Sam not trust his reads, double and triple hitch in the pocket, and toggle from risk averse to greedy at any given moment.

I don’t think Seattle will bench Darnold next week unless they make up an injury and put him on IR to heal (four games + bye week). But he’s on as short a leash as any Seahawks QB has been in a long time. Respect what Darnold did to help Seattle win a Super Bowl, but acknowledge that the context of his play and a looming extension makes his future murky. These turnovers are unacceptable.

Abe Lucas is struggling, and Josh Jones might have to start playing

This isn’t a one-off with Abe, I’m afraid. He’s been struggling badly throughout the season with pass-pro and run blocking, and Thursday night was his worst game of the season. Nik Bonitto spun him like cotton candy for one of the many sacks on Sam Darnold. He is whiffing on screens, blitzes on his side are not being picked up, and he physically looks lesser than his 2025 self.

If we’re going to talk about benching players (namely Sam Darnold), I believe changing in Josh Jones at right tackle next week should be in strong consideration. Abe is better than this and right now he’s not anywhere close to his best.

The offensive line continues to struggle

If the Seahawks aren’t going to max protect under Brian Fleury then this offensive line doesn’t have a chance. They just don’t. I am very disappointed that the OL is this underwhelming against any competent defensive line. Lucas’ struggles have already been documented, but Grey Zabel is having a second-year slump, Jalen Sundell has had his own problems in pass pro and getting bullied, and the right guard rotation continues to be an annoyance. I cannot wait until Anthony Bradford is back, a sentence I’d never thought I would type.

Klint Kubiak seemingly hid the weaknesses of this offensive line for the most part. Brian Fleury’s decreased use of max protect calls (shoutout Hawkblogger for taking Fleury to task on this) reduces help for the line and it is exposing them as not being as good as we thought they were.

Brian Fleury might be a one-and-done coordinator but in a different way

I don’t fault Fleury for the running game not being effective with below-average running backs. I fault him when Emanuel Wilson is getting short-side tosses to the weaker side of the line. Know your damn personnel. Seattle’s passing game is disjointed for reasons that are not Darnold exclusive. How many times are receivers running routes to the same area? Why are the route combinations condensing the field and adding defenders into the mix instead of spreading them out? Why is 3rd and 1 WITH TIME ON YOUR SIDE an under-center straight dropback (which was an interception)? Why is it always taking so long to get the play call in?

First-time OC, first-time playcaller, it’s an unenviable task to succeed Klint Kubiak. Some of the cracks the offense showed last season are now canyon-sized holes this season, so it’s not like some of these issues are new. That they’ve gotten worse under Fleury is not favorable for him. I’m not in “Fire Fleury” mode but I think there’s been enough dysfunction to suggest he needs to turn it around just as much as anybody.

The Rashid Shaheed contract looks like a disaster

Shaheed was a good player for the New Orleans Saints and a valuable part of Seattle’s Super Bowl run last year, albeit primarily through special teams. He does not fit this offense and possibly not this quarterback. The 5-catch showing flatters him, and if nothing else I think his two-point conversion catch was his best play all night. But he also lost a fumble and then had a pretty important dropped kickoff to start overtime that, combined with a Tyrice Knight holding penalty, backed Seattle up at its 11.

I’ve way over-estimated Seattle’s wide receiver group outside of JSN. The 2026 version of Cooper Kupp is still capable but can’t be your WR2. Tory Horton has not justified a high target share and I think he has some culpability on the first interception. Shaheed’s contract involved more offensive productivity that isn’t happening, and he’s now fumbled three kickoffs in five weeks, which I’m not thrilled with even though he had a couple of big returns.

It may not happen this year, but I don’t see how Shaheed sees out his contract here. I say this as a fan of his but it looks like this is a miscalculated mismatch.

Mike Macdonald needs to own this team’s perennial turnover woes under his watch

I almost never put Coach Macdonald in the Losers. I will now. The Seahawks have turned it over 64 times under Macdonald, which is ridiculous given he’s only coached 40 regular season games. Are a lot of these turnovers on Geno Smith and Sam? Yes. But Seattle’s ball security has consistently been atrocious and the Seahawks cannot go a game without fumbling.

Macdonald’s attention to detail on defense is second to none. The offense (and, at times, special teams) consistently being mistake prone and charitable with the ball is a literal Day 1 problem since he’s been head coach. It’s the total opposite of Pete Carroll’s almost overly obsessive belief in low turnovers. You’re not going to have an elite defense every year to keep you in games. These will become blowout losses if Seattle doesn’t rectify this.

John Schneider got the running back re-tooling wrong

Not re-signing Kenneth Walker III in itself is not indefensible. It’s what happened afterward that I think needs re-examination. Zach Charbonnet being out for half the year means that the Seahawks gambled on the first half of the season being a “by-committee” approach between Jadarian Price, Emanuel Wilson, and George Holani. There isn’t a proven RB1 in that trio and the latter two are not and never will be regular starting RBs. Price has shown promise and him getting hurt is bad luck, but Seattle chose the one early-round back without any heavy workload history.

You can get away with rotating guy who are starting caliber like Walker and Charbonnet and run a functioning offense. You can’t do that with the backs they actually have while Charbonnet is still hurt. And with Price hurt? Yards are being left on the field by Wilson and Holani through little fault of their own; they’re being asked to do more than what they’re capable of. Emanuel Wilson is Wario K9: He’s not fast, he doesn’t make people miss, but my god he will run the play as intended. You’ll never have to complain about Wilson freestyling when he shouldn’t. But you ain’t getting an extra yard than what the play is expected to get.

This is the 2017 offensive line but for the running back position. I think Schneider got this wrong and I don’t say it with full hindsight, because I wanted the Seahawks to sign Tyler Allgeier or someone who has some level of starting experience. We got what we got.

Final Notes

  • Jason Myers narrowly avoided the losers list for his part in missing a field goal and nearly missing the tying one for overtime. If it’s not one thing it’s another with this inconsistent special teams unit.
  • Sorry, I don’t have the energy for anymore. It’s 11:25 pm PT. If you put me in a position to predict whether the Seahawks make the playoffs or not, I lean towards no. Somewhere in the 10-7 or 9-8 range and that might not be enough in the NFC. I understand the 49ers and Broncos are a tough two-game combo on a short week, but they’re been pretty sloppy with normal rest. If it’s not penalties, it’s turnovers, it’s drops, it’s just bad ball. I don’t see how they beat the Kansas City Chiefs next week, and nothing would be more fitting than K9 rushing for over 100 yards and ending Seattle’s streak of not allowing a 100-yard rusher. This mini-bye is the biggest test of Macdonald as a coach, because this “run it forward” season is only running head-on into a brick wall, Wile E. Coyote style.
